questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is studying the synthesis and secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin). Which of the following correctly describes the anatomic site of ADH synthesis and release?
choices: ADH is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary
ADH is synthesized in the anterior pituitary
ADH is synthesized in the adrenal cortex
ADH is synthesized in the kidney itself
ADH is synthesized in the heart
explanations: Correct. ADH (vasopressin) is a 9-amino-acid peptide synthesized in magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic nucleus (SON) and paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus. It is packaged in granules with its carrier protein neurophysin II and transported by axonal transport down to the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis), where it is released into systemic circulation. Stimuli for release include: (1) elevated plasma osmolality (sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors at threshold ~280 mOsm/kg; very sensitive — small changes detected); (2) reduced effective arterial volume (sensed by arterial baroreceptors in carotid sinus/aortic arch and by low-pressure stretch receptors in atria; less sensitive but more potent at extremes — severe hypovolemia overrides osmotic suppression). Pituitary stalk transection above the median eminence does NOT cause permanent DI because ADH-secreting axons proximal to the lesion can still release ADH into the median eminence.
Incorrect. The anterior pituitary secretes ACTH, GH, TSH, prolactin, FSH, LH — but NOT ADH.
Incorrect. ADH is hypothalamic, not adrenal.
Incorrect. The kidney does not synthesize ADH; it is the target organ.
Incorrect. The heart secretes natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP), not ADH.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old physiologist is studying the receptor subtypes for vasopressin. Which of the following correctly characterizes the major vasopressin receptor subtypes and their tissue distribution?
choices: All vasopressin receptors are V1 receptors
V1 on vascular smooth muscle; V2 in collecting duct principal cells
V3 receptor is the principal renal water-handling receptor
explanations: Incorrect. Vasopressin has multiple receptor subtypes with distinct functions and tissue distributions.

Correct. Vasopressin acts at three principal receptor subtypes: (1) V1a (or V1) — on vascular smooth muscle (Gq-coupled, raising IP3/DAG/Ca2+; produces vasoconstriction), platelets (aggregation), hepatocytes (glycogenolysis); (2) V1b (also called V3) — in the anterior pituitary (stimulates ACTH release in response to stress); (3) V2 — in collecting duct principal cells (Gs-coupled, raising cAMP; triggers AQP2 trafficking and water reabsorption). The V2 receptor is the principal renal water-handling target. Selective V2 antagonists (tolvaptan, conivaptan) treat hyponatremia from SIADH without producing the cardiovascular effects of V1 antagonism. V1 effects are exploited therapeutically with vasopressin or terlipressin in septic shock, hepatorenal syndrome, and esophageal variceal bleeding.
Incorrect. V2 (not V1) mediates renal water reabsorption.
Incorrect. V1 (not V2) mediates vasoconstriction.
Incorrect. V3 is in the anterior pituitary (ACTH release), not the kidney.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher studies the mechanism by which ADH increases water permeability in collecting duct principal cells. The diagram below summarizes the V2 receptor signaling pathway. Which of the following correctly describes the molecular sequence by which ADH increases collecting duct water permeability?
questions.diagram:
V2-receptor signaling in collecting duct principal cell
ADH → V2 receptor (basolateral)
→ Gs / adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cytoplasmic cAMP
→ PKA activation → phosphorylation of AQP2-containing vesicles
→ Vesicle trafficking and apical insertion of AQP2 water channels
→ Water enters cell apically (AQP2), exits basolaterally (AQP3, AQP4) → reabsorbed
choices: ADH binds an apical receptor and directly opens AQP2
ADH activates Na+/K+-ATPase, secondarily moving water
ADH binds basolateral V2 → cAMP → PKA → AQP2 trafficking
ADH directly synthesizes new AQP2 protein within minutes
explanations: Incorrect. ADH binds the BASOLATERAL V2 receptor (not apical); it does not directly open AQP2.
Incorrect. ADH does not activate Na+/K+-ATPase; the water reabsorption is osmotic.

Correct. The classical V2-receptor signaling cascade: (1) ADH (vasopressin) binds the V2 receptor on the BASOLATERAL membrane of collecting duct principal cells; (2) the Gs-coupled receptor activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cytoplasmic cAMP; (3) cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA); (4) PKA phosphorylates AQP2-containing intracellular vesicles (and other proteins) signaling them to traffic to the apical membrane; (5) AQP2 vesicles fuse with the apical membrane, inserting AQP2 water channels; (6) water now flows from the tubular lumen into the cell down the osmotic gradient (set by the medullary interstitium); (7) water exits the cell via the constitutively expressed basolateral AQP3 and AQP4 channels and enters the peritubular interstitium and circulation. Within minutes of ADH withdrawal, AQP2 is endocytosed back into vesicles, returning water permeability to baseline.
Incorrect. AQP2 protein is preformed in vesicles; ADH triggers TRAFFICKING, not new synthesis (within minutes; chronic ADH does upregulate AQP2 transcription).
Incorrect. ADH does not close ENaC; it acts through V2 → AQP2 trafficking.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man develops central diabetes insipidus following pituitary surgery. Compared with a healthy individual at baseline, which row in the table best describes the changes in plasma osmolality, plasma ADH, and urine osmolality in this patient?
explanations: Correct. Central DI is characterized by deficient ADH secretion (despite intact target tissue). The classic pattern: (1) plasma ADH is INAPPROPRIATELY LOW (or absent) — this is the primary defect; (2) without ADH-driven AQP2 trafficking, the collecting duct cannot reabsorb water, so urine osmolality is LOW (dilute, often <300 mOsm/kg); (3) free water loss leads to hypernatremia and HIGH plasma osmolality. Treatment is exogenous desmopressin (DDAVP, a V2-selective synthetic ADH analog), which fully reverses the urinary concentrating defect.
Incorrect. ↑Posm + ↑ADH + ↑Uosm describes APPROPRIATE response to volume depletion or osmotic stimulus — opposite of central DI.
Incorrect. ↓Posm + ↑ADH + ↑Uosm describes SIADH (inappropriate ADH despite low plasma osmolality).
Incorrect. ↓Posm + ↓ADH + ↓Uosm describes water excess with appropriately suppressed ADH (e.g., primary polydipsia).
Incorrect. Unchanged values describe a healthy individual.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher measures plasma ADH at varying plasma osmolalities. Which of the following best describes the OSMOTIC THRESHOLD for ADH secretion in healthy adults?
explanations: Incorrect. 250 is well below the threshold; ADH would be fully suppressed at this osmolality.
Incorrect. 270 is below the threshold (which is ~280).
Incorrect. 285 is in the normal range; ADH secretion has begun by then but is not the threshold itself.

Correct. The osmotic threshold for ADH secretion in healthy adults is approximately 280 mOsm/kg. Below this, ADH secretion is essentially fully suppressed (allowing maximal water diuresis when needed). Above this, plasma ADH rises progressively — approximately linearly — with plasma osmolality, until a plateau at higher levels. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors are very sensitive: a 1–2% change in plasma osmolality (~3–5 mOsm/kg) is detected. The thirst threshold is slightly higher (~290), so ADH-mediated water conservation is engaged before subjective thirst is felt. Both thresholds shift with conditions: pregnancy lowers the threshold; aging raises it (contributing to increased risk of dehydration in elderly). The osmotic regulation of ADH is the principal mechanism for tonicity homeostasis under most physiologic conditions.
Incorrect. 310 is well ABOVE threshold; ADH would be markedly elevated at this level.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with class III hemorrhagic shock has plasma osmolality 282 mOsm/kg (essentially normal) but plasma ADH is markedly elevated. Which of the following best explains the ADH elevation in this scenario?
choices: Plasma osmolality is misleading — it must be high to elevate ADH
Volume stimuli to ADH override osmotic suppression
explanations: Incorrect. Reset osmostat is a chronic phenomenon with shifted threshold; this is acute hemorrhage with appropriate ADH response.
Incorrect. SIADH features inappropriate ADH despite low plasma osmolality and euvolemia; this patient is hypovolemic.
Incorrect. The pattern is internally consistent with appropriate volume-driven ADH response.
Incorrect. Volume stimuli can drive ADH at any osmolality.

Correct. ADH is regulated by TWO classes of stimuli: (1) OSMOTIC — hypothalamic osmoreceptors are very sensitive (<2% change detected); ADH rises modestly with plasma osmolality. (2) VOLUME / PRESSURE — arterial baroreceptors (carotid sinus, aortic arch) and low-pressure stretch receptors (atria, pulmonary veins) sense reduced effective arterial volume. Volume sensors are LESS sensitive (small changes don't trigger them) but MORE potent at extremes — severe hypovolemia (≥10–20% volume loss) produces ADH levels 50–100× the maximum osmotic response. Volume stimuli can OVERRIDE osmotic suppression: in shock, severe HF, or cirrhosis, ADH may be elevated EVEN WHEN plasma osmolality is LOW (driving the hyponatremia of these states). Recognizing this is critical: treating hyponatremia in HF requires addressing the underlying low EAV, not simply restricting free water.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old healthy man is fluid-deprived for 24 hours. His ADH-driven concentrating mechanism is fully intact. Which of the following best approximates the maximum urine osmolality his kidney can achieve?
explanations: Correct. The healthy human kidney can concentrate urine to approximately 1,200 mOsm/kg under maximum ADH stimulation — about 4× plasma osmolality. The mechanism requires three intact systems: (1) maximal ADH-mediated AQP2 insertion in collecting duct principal cells; (2) the medullary osmotic gradient generated by countercurrent multiplication in the loops of Henle; (3) urea recycling in the inner medullary collecting duct (UT-A1, UT-A3 transporters), which contributes substantially to inner medullary osmolality. Maximum concentrating ability declines with age; impaired by loop diuretics (impair countercurrent), lithium and demeclocycline (impair AQP2), hypercalcemia, hypokalemia (downregulate AQP2), and chronic medullary disease.
Incorrect. 50 mOsm/kg is the MINIMUM (during maximal water diuresis), not maximum.
Incorrect. 100 mOsm/kg approaches minimum, not maximum.
Incorrect. 300 mOsm/kg is approximately ISOSMOTIC with plasma — neither concentrated nor dilute.
Incorrect. 600 mOsm/kg is concentrated but well below maximum.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman drinks 3 L of water rapidly as part of a research protocol. ADH is appropriately suppressed. Which of the following best approximates the minimum urine osmolality her kidney can produce?
explanations: Incorrect. 600 mOsm/kg is concentrated, not dilute.

Correct. The healthy young human kidney can dilute urine to approximately 50 mOsm/kg during maximal water diuresis (when ADH is fully suppressed). Mechanism: (1) ADH suppression keeps AQP2 internalized in collecting duct principal cells, preventing water reabsorption; (2) the thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl from tubular fluid into the medullary interstitium WITHOUT water (water-impermeable), generating hypotonic fluid that flows to the collecting duct; (3) without ADH, this dilute fluid is excreted essentially unchanged. Minimum urine osmolality rises with: aging (commonly only down to ~100 in older adults), loop diuretics (block TAL diluting function), thiazides (block DCT), and any state with inappropriate ADH (SIADH, severe HF, cirrhosis). The diluting capacity sets the ceiling for water excretion (~18–20 L/day in healthy young adults; less in elderly).
Incorrect. 300 mOsm/kg is iso-osmotic with plasma; the kidney can dilute below this.
Incorrect. 150 mOsm/kg is more concentrated than the minimum the kidney can achieve.
Incorrect. 1,200 mOsm/kg is the MAXIMUM concentration, not minimum.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is studying the regulation of thirst in healthy volunteers. Which of the following best characterizes the regulation of thirst?
choices: Thirst is regulated independently of ADH
Thirst is regulated solely by mouth dryness
Thirst threshold is much lower than ADH threshold
Thirst is independent of plasma osmolality
explanations: Incorrect. Thirst and ADH are coupled, both responding to osmotic and volume stimuli.
Incorrect. Mouth dryness contributes peripherally but the principal regulation is central (hypothalamic).

Correct. Thirst is regulated principally by hypothalamic osmoreceptors located in circumventricular organs (organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis, OVLT; subfornical organ, SFO) — small areas of the hypothalamus that lack a blood-brain barrier and can directly sense plasma osmolality. The osmotic threshold for thirst is ~290 mOsm/kg, slightly higher than the ADH threshold (~280) — so ADH-mediated water conservation kicks in BEFORE subjective thirst is felt. Thirst is also driven by reduced effective arterial volume (volume-mediated thirst) and by angiotensin II (which has direct dipsogenic effects). Both pathways converge on the hypothalamic centers to drive water-seeking behavior. Aging blunts both thirst threshold and thirst response (a major contributor to dehydration in elderly).
Incorrect. Thirst threshold is HIGHER than ADH threshold (~290 vs ~280).
Incorrect. Plasma osmolality is the principal stimulus for thirst.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with central diabetes insipidus is being evaluated for an underlying cause. Which of the following is the most common etiology of central DI in an adult?
explanations: Incorrect. Familial central DI (autosomal dominant; AVP-NPII gene mutation) is RARE; idiopathic and acquired causes dominate.
Incorrect. Lithium causes NEPHROGENIC DI (kidney resistance to ADH), not central DI.
Incorrect. Hypercalcemia causes NEPHROGENIC DI by impairing AQP2 trafficking, not central DI.

Correct. The principal causes of central DI are: (1) idiopathic/autoimmune (~30%, recognized as autoimmune destruction of vasopressinergic neurons in many cases); (2) traumatic — pituitary surgery, traumatic stalk transection (often after head injury); (3) neoplastic — craniopharyngioma (children), metastatic disease (lung, breast cancer), pituitary macroadenoma with stalk effect, lymphoma, germinoma; (4) infiltrative — sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, hemochromatosis; (5) vascular — Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis), aneurysm; (6) inherited — autosomal dominant AVP-NPII gene mutation (familial neurohypophyseal DI; rare); (7) drugs — phenytoin (rare). MRI of the pituitary (looking for absent posterior pituitary 'bright spot' and stalk thickening) is the principal imaging study.
Incorrect. Pregnancy can cause TRANSIENT central DI from placental vasopressinase, but this is uncommon and usually resolves postpartum.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with polyuria of 6 L/day and polydipsia for 3 weeks following pituitary surgery for a craniopharyngioma. He undergoes a water deprivation test. Laboratory studies are shown.

labs.name: Urine osm 1 h after IM desmopressin

explanations: Incorrect. Primary polydipsia would show urine concentration WITH water deprivation alone (without need for desmopressin); this patient failed to concentrate.
Incorrect. Nephrogenic DI fails to concentrate urine even AFTER desmopressin; this patient's urine osm rose from 150 to 650 (>50% rise), confirming central rather than nephrogenic.
Incorrect. SIADH features euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine despite low plasma osmolality; this patient has hypernatremia and dilute urine.
Incorrect. Reset osmostat is a stable but altered set point; it does not produce frank polyuria with dilute urine.

Correct. Water deprivation test sequence in central DI: (1) baseline urine is dilute (85) despite normal-high plasma osmolality (292); (2) water deprivation raises plasma osmolality (308) but the kidney still cannot concentrate urine (Uosm 150) — confirming the inappropriate response; (3) IM desmopressin (synthetic V2 agonist) produces dramatic increase in urine osmolality (≥50% rise) — confirming that the V2 receptor and AQP2 machinery are intact. Treatment: long-term desmopressin (intranasal, oral, or SC), oral fluid replacement, and addressing the underlying cause (postoperative DI may be transient — 'triphasic response' with initial DI, transient SIADH-like phase, then permanent DI in some patients).

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on chronic lithium therapy develops polyuria of 5 L/day. Plasma sodium is 148 mEq/L; urine osmolality is 80 mOsm/kg even after water deprivation; desmopressin produces NO change in urine osmolality. Which of the following best characterizes the underlying disorder?
choices: Central DI from lithium-induced pituitary damage
explanations: Correct. Lithium-induced nephrogenic DI is the most common ACQUIRED NDI in adults, occurring in up to 40% of patients on chronic lithium. Mechanism: lithium enters collecting duct principal cells via apical ENaC (lithium is a small monovalent cation handled like Na+) and accumulates intracellularly. Once intracellular, lithium inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) and other signaling pathways involved in AQP2 trafficking. Chronic lithium also reduces AQP2 expression at the protein level and produces histologic tubulointerstitial changes (tubular atrophy, microcysts). The water deprivation test pattern is diagnostic: urine fails to concentrate after deprivation AND fails to concentrate after desmopressin (the kidney itself doesn't respond). Reversible if lithium discontinued early; can be irreversible after years. Treatment: (1) discontinue lithium if possible; (2) amiloride blocks ENaC and prevents lithium uptake into principal cells (allows patients to continue lithium); (3) thiazides produce paradoxical antidiuresis via volume contraction → enhanced proximal water reabsorption.
Incorrect. Lithium does not cause central DI; the lesion is at the kidney.
Incorrect. SIADH would feature HYPOnatremia, not hypernatremia.
Incorrect. Reset osmostat is a stable set-point change without polyuria.
Incorrect. Familial X-linked NDI typically presents in male infants with severe polyuria; not a 50-year-old on lithium.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with metastatic squamous cell lung cancer has hypercalcemia (calcium 13.5 mg/dL) and presents with polyuria. Plasma sodium is 148 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
choices: Hypercalcemia activates the calcium-sensing receptor in principal cells
Hypercalcemia destroys the medullary gradient via direct mechanical effects
Hypercalcemia causes central DI via pituitary stalk damage
explanations: Incorrect. Hypercalcemia does not stimulate ADH; if anything, it impairs renal response to ADH.

Correct. Hypercalcemia produces nephrogenic DI through activation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), which is expressed in two key sites in the kidney: (1) basolateral membrane of collecting duct principal cells — CaSR activation inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reducing cAMP-driven AQP2 trafficking even in the presence of normal ADH; (2) basolateral membrane of thick ascending limb cells — CaSR activation reduces NKCC2 activity, impairing the medullary osmotic gradient. Chronic hypercalcemia also downregulates AQP2 protein expression. The result is impaired water reabsorption AND impaired medullary gradient — both contributing to nephrogenic DI. Correcting hypercalcemia typically restores concentrating ability, though slowly (days to weeks).
Incorrect. The mechanism is molecular (CaSR-mediated), not mechanical.
Incorrect. Hypercalcemia does not cause central DI through pituitary damage.
Incorrect. Hypercalcemia does not increase ADH degradation.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic diarrhea and severe hypokalemia (K+ 2.4 mEq/L) develops polyuria. Plasma osmolality is 295 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 180. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of hypokalemia-induced nephrogenic DI?
choices: Hypokalemia destroys collecting duct principal cells
Severe chronic hypokalemia downregulates AQP2 expression
explanations: Incorrect. Hypokalemia does not principally stimulate ADH; the issue is renal responsiveness.
Incorrect. Hypokalemia does not destroy principal cells; the lesion is functional.

Correct. Severe chronic hypokalemia produces an acquired nephrogenic DI through several mechanisms: (1) downregulation of AQP2 expression in collecting duct principal cells; (2) intracellular acidosis from reduced K+ gradient impairs AQP2 trafficking and may reduce V2 receptor sensitivity; (3) concurrent reduction in NKCC2 activity in the TAL (because reduced K+ availability limits cotransport) impairs the medullary osmotic gradient. The kidney becomes resistant to ADH despite normal levels. Polyuria is typically modest (2–4 L/day) and usually resolves with K+ replacement, although recovery can take days to weeks. Severe chronic hypokalemia (e.g., from chronic diarrhea, diuretics, Bartter/Gitelman syndromes) is the typical setting; the polyuria may go unnoticed if attributed to other causes.
Incorrect. Hypokalemia causes nephrogenic, not central, DI.
Incorrect. The principal effect is AQP2 downregulation and trafficking impairment, not specifically endocytosis.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old male infant presents with profound polyuria of 4 L/day, severe dehydration, hypernatremia (Na+ 168), and failure to thrive. His mother had a brother with similar findings who died in infancy. Water deprivation fails to concentrate urine; desmopressin produces no response. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Familial central DI (autosomal dominant AVP-NPII gene mutation)
Acquired nephrogenic DI from drug toxicity
explanations: Incorrect. Familial central DI would respond to desmopressin (V2 receptor and AQP2 are intact); this patient does not respond.
Incorrect. There is no drug exposure described; the family history strongly suggests inherited disease.
Incorrect. SIADH features hyponatremia and concentrated urine; this patient has hypernatremia and dilute urine.

Correct. X-linked nephrogenic DI is the most common HEREDITARY form of nephrogenic DI (~90%). Loss-of-function mutations in the AVPR2 gene (encoding the V2 receptor) on Xq28 produce non-functional or absent V2 receptors. Affected males (hemizygous) present in infancy with severe polyuria, dehydration, hypernatremia, irritability, vomiting, and failure to thrive. Family history typical: maternal uncles or male relatives affected (X-linked). Female carriers may show variable expression due to skewed X-inactivation. Water deprivation test: fails to concentrate urine, AND no response to desmopressin (since V2 receptor is non-functional). Treatment: aggressive free water access; thiazide diuretic (paradoxical antidiuresis via volume contraction → enhanced proximal water reabsorption); amiloride may be added; low-salt diet. With appropriate management, growth and development normalize. Other inherited NDI (autosomal recessive AQP2 mutation, ~10%) is clinically similar but rarer.
Incorrect. Primary polydipsia is uncommon in infants and would show urinary concentration after water deprivation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has plasma sodium 142 mEq/L and urine osmolality 380 mOsm/kg after an overnight water deprivation. Her physician suspects partial central DI rather than complete central DI. Which of the following best characterizes partial central DI compared with complete central DI?
choices: Partial central DI is more severe than complete central DI
Partial central DI does not respond to desmopressin
Partial central DI features absent ADH
Partial central DI has normal urine concentrating ability
Partial central DI features residual but inadequate ADH secretion
explanations: Incorrect. Partial central DI is LESS severe (residual ADH) than complete central DI.
Incorrect. Partial central DI DOES respond to desmopressin (since V2 and AQP2 are intact).
Incorrect. Partial DI features RESIDUAL ADH; complete DI has absent ADH.
Incorrect. Partial central DI has IMPAIRED concentrating ability (incomplete), not normal.

Correct. Central DI exists on a spectrum. Complete central DI (severe, residual ADH minimal): no urinary concentration even with severe water deprivation; full response to desmopressin (additive concentration to maximum). Partial central DI (more common, milder): residual ADH-secreting neurons provide some concentration after deprivation (Uosm typically 300–700 mOsm/kg, incomplete) but inadequate for normal water balance; further response to desmopressin (additional 10–50% rise in Uosm). The water deprivation test distinguishes them by quantitative response. Both respond to desmopressin treatment; partial DI may require lower doses. Other distinguishing factor from partial nephrogenic DI: partial NDI also has incomplete concentration after deprivation but LESS response to desmopressin (typically <10% additional rise).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is being evaluated for polyuria. Water deprivation test results are shown. Compared with reference patterns for various disorders, which row best matches her results?
explanations: Incorrect. Row A: high baseline Posm, dilute urine after deprivation, RESPONDS to desmopressin — this is CENTRAL DI (the V2/AQP2 machinery is intact; the lesion is at ADH secretion).

Correct (assuming the patient's results match this pattern). Row B describes NEPHROGENIC DI: high baseline Posm (from water loss), dilute urine after deprivation (kidney cannot concentrate), and NO RESPONSE to desmopressin (the V2 receptor or AQP2 itself is dysfunctional, so synthetic ADH agonist is ineffective). Causes: hereditary (X-linked AVPR2 mutation, AQP2 mutation), acquired (lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, post-obstructive). Treatment differs from central DI — desmopressin doesn't work; instead use thiazide ± amiloride (paradoxical antidiuresis) and address underlying cause.
Incorrect. Row C: low Posm with concentrated urine — this is SIADH (inappropriately concentrated urine despite low plasma osmolality and euvolemic hyponatremia).

Incorrect. Row D: low-normal Posm with concentrated urine after deprivation — this is PRIMARY POLYDIPSIA (excessive water intake suppresses ADH, but dehydration during deprivation allows urinary concentration).
Incorrect. Row E: normal Posm with high baseline urine osmolality, no further rise with desmopressin — this is HEALTHY (already maximally concentrated).

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer presents with euvolemic hyponatremia. Plasma sodium 122 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 252 mOsm/kg. Urine osmolality is 580 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 80 mEq/L. He is clinically euvolemic. Which of the following best characterizes SIADH?
choices: Inappropriately elevated ADH despite low plasma osmolality
explanations: Incorrect. Volume depletion would feature physical signs of hypovolemia and elevated BUN:Cr, neither described here.

Correct. SIADH is the syndrome of INAPPROPRIATELY ELEVATED ADH despite low plasma osmolality and adequate volume status. Diagnostic criteria (Schwartz-Bartter): (1) plasma osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; (2) inappropriately concentrated urine (Uosm >100 mOsm/kg, usually >300); (3) clinical euvolemia; (4) urinary sodium ≥40 mEq/L on normal sodium intake; (5) exclusion of thyroid, adrenal, and renal causes; (6) no recent diuretic use. Causes: (a) paraneoplastic — especially small cell lung cancer (~70% of paraneoplastic SIADH; ectopic ADH secretion by tumor); also pancreatic, prostate, lymphoma; (b) CNS disorders — stroke (especially SAH), hemorrhage, infection, trauma; (c) pulmonary disease — pneumonia (especially Legionella), tuberculosis, lung abscess, ARDS; (d) drugs — SSRIs (especially fluoxetine in elderly), carbamazepine, vincristine, MDMA (ecstasy), chemotherapeutics; (e) idiopathic. Treatment: free water restriction; hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic; tolvaptan or demeclocycline for chronic management.
Incorrect. CHF presents with HYPERVOLEMIC hyponatremia (edema, JVD).
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia features NORMAL plasma osmolality.
Incorrect. Primary polydipsia features DILUTE urine (suppressed ADH); this patient has CONCENTRATED urine.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer is admitted with confusion. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: SIADH from paraneoplastic ectopic ADH production
explanations: Incorrect. HF presents with hypervolemic hyponatremia (edema, JVD); this patient is euvolemic.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease (SAH, TBI); this patient has SCLC, not CNS pathology.

Correct. Classic SIADH from paraneoplastic ectopic ADH secretion by small cell lung cancer. The diagnostic criteria are met: plasma osmolality <275 mOsm/kg (245), inappropriately concentrated urine (Uosm 640, far higher than plasma osm of 245), urine Na+ ≥40 mEq/L (92, reflecting normal renal Na+ handling and Na+ excretion to match free water gain), euvolemic on examination, and exclusion of thyroid/adrenal causes. SCLC is the most common malignancy associated with paraneoplastic SIADH (~70% of paraneoplastic cases). Management of severe symptomatic hyponatremia (Na+ <125 with confusion, seizures): IV hypertonic 3% saline boluses (100 mL over 10 min, may repeat up to 3×) to acutely raise plasma Na+ by 4–6 mEq/L within first few hours; transition to free water restriction (≤800 mL/day) ± tolvaptan for chronic management. CRITICAL: limit total correction to ≤8 mEq/L in 24 hours (or ≤10 in some settings) to avoid OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME (formerly central pontine myelinolysis), particularly in chronic hyponatremia.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia features NORMAL plasma osmolality (laboratory artifact); this patient has clearly LOW plasma osm (245).
Incorrect. Hyperglycemic hyponatremia features HIGH plasma osmolality from glucose; this patient's osm is low.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic SIADH from small cell lung cancer is being managed long-term. Free water restriction alone has been inadequate to maintain plasma sodium >130. The team considers tolvaptan vs demeclocycline. Which of the following best characterizes these agents?
choices: Demeclocycline is a tetracycline antibiotic that induces nephrogenic DI
Both lower urine osmolality but only demeclocycline is V2-specific
Both have approximately equal renal effect and tolerance
Tolvaptan is a V2 antagonist; demeclocycline induces nephrogenic DI
explanations: Incorrect. Tolvaptan IS a V2 antagonist, but the BEST answer characterizes BOTH drugs.
Incorrect. Demeclocycline IS a tetracycline that induces NDI, but the BEST answer characterizes BOTH drugs together.
Incorrect. Tolvaptan is the V2-specific agent; demeclocycline is non-specific.
Incorrect. The two drugs have important differences in mechanism, specificity, and side effects.

Correct. Both drugs treat SIADH but differ markedly. (1) TOLVAPTAN — a competitive V2-receptor antagonist that prevents ADH-mediated AQP2 trafficking. Produces 'aquaresis' — selective water diuresis without significant Na+/K+ loss. Rapid onset, dose-titratable, predictable. Modern preferred agent for chronic SIADH refractory to free water restriction. Limitations: cost, liver toxicity (FDA black-box warning for ADPKD use; some hepatotoxicity reports in SIADH patients, hence treatment limited to 30 days), and concerns about overly rapid Na+ correction. (2) DEMECLOCYCLINE — a tetracycline antibiotic discovered to induce nephrogenic DI by impairing AQP2 trafficking. Older, non-specific, less predictable. Side effects include tetracycline-class GI effects, photosensitivity, dental staining (avoid in children/pregnancy), and nephrotoxicity (especially with cirrhosis). Now largely superseded by tolvaptan but still used in some patients.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with schizophrenia drinks 8 L of water per day, has plasma sodium 124, and presents with confusion. Laboratory studies are shown.
explanations: Incorrect. SIADH would feature CONCENTRATED urine (>100 mOsm/kg, usually >300); this patient has markedly DILUTE urine (75).
Incorrect. CSW features hypovolemia and high urine Na+ (>40); this patient is euvolemic with normal-low urine Na+.
Incorrect. NDI features HYPERnatremia and dilute urine; this patient has HYPOnatremia.
Incorrect. Reset osmostat features stable but altered set point with concentrated urine; this patient has dilute urine.

Correct. Primary polydipsia (psychogenic polydipsia) is excessive compulsive water intake that overwhelms the kidney's diluting capacity (~18–20 L/day in healthy young adults; less in elderly). Common in patients with schizophrenia (10–20%) and other psychiatric disorders; also occurs in some healthy individuals. Diagnostic features: HYPONATREMIA (from water dilution), LOW plasma osmolality (from same), MARKEDLY DILUTE urine (Uosm <100; the kidney is appropriately suppressing ADH and excreting maximal free water — this is the key differentiator from SIADH), normal-low urine sodium (no specific renal abnormality). The kidney is acting appropriately; the problem is excessive intake. Distinguishes from SIADH (concentrated urine due to inappropriate ADH) and from DI (hypernatremia, dilute urine). Treatment: water restriction, behavioral interventions; severe cases may need limited water access; sodium repletion is generally not needed since correction occurs with restriction. Avoid rapid Na+ correction in chronic primary polydipsia to prevent osmotic demyelination.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman with central DI from a prior craniopharyngioma is admitted with hypernatremia (Na+ 168). She weighs 60 kg. The team is calculating her free water deficit. Which of the following formulas correctly approximates the free water deficit?
choices: Water deficit = TBW × [(measured Na+ / desired Na+) − 1]
Water deficit = serum Na+ × body weight / 100
explanations: Correct. Water deficit (L) = TBW × [(measured Na+ / desired Na+) − 1], where TBW ≈ 60% body weight in adult men, 50% in adult women, 75% in infants, lower in elderly and obese. For this 75-year-old woman at 60 kg: TBW = 0.5 × 60 = 30 L (using 50% for adult women); Na+ ratio = 168/140 = 1.2, so deficit factor = 0.2; water deficit = 30 × 0.2 = 6 L. (Some clinicians use 0.45 for elderly women due to reduced TBW%.) Correction principles: (1) replace half the deficit over the first 24 hours, the remainder over the next 24–72 hours; (2) limit the rate of Na+ correction to ≤10 mEq/L/24h (≤0.5 mEq/L/hr) to avoid cerebral edema; (3) account for ongoing losses (insensible, urinary, GI); (4) IV D5W or 0.45% saline; oral water acceptable if tolerated; (5) add desmopressin to address ongoing renal water loss in central DI.
Incorrect. This formula is invented; not the standard.
Incorrect. Not the correct formula.
Incorrect. 0.6 × body weight is TBW for men (not the deficit calculation).
Incorrect. Not the standard formula.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia who has been compulsively drinking 10 L of water per day for years has plasma sodium 118 mEq/L on admission. She has been told her hyponatremia must be corrected. The team is concerned about overcorrection. Which of the following best characterizes the appropriate correction rate to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome?
choices: Correct as fast as possible to >135
Correction rate should be 25 mEq/L per 24 hours
Correction rate of 15 mEq/L per 24 hours is safe
explanations: Incorrect. Rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination syndrome.

Correct. Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS, formerly central pontine myelinolysis or CPM) is a feared complication of overly rapid correction of CHRONIC hyponatremia. Mechanism: in chronic hyponatremia (>48 hours), brain cells defend their volume by losing idiogenic osmoles (myo-inositol, glutamine, taurine, etc.) — reducing intracellular osmolality to match the lowered ECF osmolality. Rapid restoration of plasma Na+ shifts water OUT of brain cells rapidly (faster than the cells can rebuild lost osmoles), causing intracellular dehydration and demyelination — particularly in pons and extrapontine sites. Symptoms: dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis, locked-in syndrome — often delayed 1–7 days after correction; can be devastating and irreversible. Correction limits to avoid ODS: ≤8 mEq/L/24 hours (some guidelines say ≤10 in very acute hyponatremia), with ≤6 mEq/L/24h preferred in high-risk patients (chronic alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia, severe Na+ depression, hepatic disease). If correction is initially too fast, DDAVP can be re-introduced to slow further rise. ACUTE hyponatremia (<48 hours) carries less ODS risk because brain idiogenic osmoles haven't been depleted yet — but is still corrected cautiously.
Incorrect. 25 mEq/L/24h is far too rapid and would risk severe ODS.
Incorrect. 15 mEq/L/24h exceeds the safe limit.
Incorrect. Symptomatic hyponatremia at Na+ 118 requires correction; the question is RATE, not whether to correct.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher is studying brain adaptation to chronic hyponatremia. Which of the following best characterizes the brain's response to sustained hyponatremia (>48 hours)?
choices: Brain cells lose K+ to reduce intracellular osmolality
Brain cells gain K+ to increase intracellular osmolality
Brain cells lose idiogenic osmoles to defend volume
explanations: Incorrect. Brain cells lose ORGANIC osmolytes (idiogenic osmoles), not principally K+, to defend volume.
Incorrect. Gaining osmoles would WORSEN brain edema in hyponatremia; brain cells lose them.

Correct. Chronic hyponatremia (>48 hours) triggers brain adaptive volume defense. The adaptation works by loss of organic osmolytes (idiogenic osmoles): myo-inositol, glutamine, taurine, glutamate, glycerophosphocholine, and others. By extruding these solutes, brain cells reduce their intracellular osmolality to match the lowered ECF osmolality — preventing osmotic water entry and brain edema. This protective mechanism explains why chronic hyponatremia is often less symptomatic than acute hyponatremia at the same plasma Na+ level. CRITICAL CONSEQUENCE: rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia shifts water out of brain cells before the lost osmoles can be replenished (recovery of idiogenic osmoles takes days), causing intracellular dehydration and pontine/extrapontine demyelination — osmotic demyelination syndrome. This is why correction is limited to ≤8 mEq/L/24h in chronic hyponatremia. Acute hyponatremia (<48 hours) — where brain hasn't adapted yet — has both higher symptom burden (cerebral edema) AND lower ODS risk during correction.
Incorrect. Aquaporin production is not the principal adaptation.
Incorrect. Brain DOES adapt to chronic hyponatremia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with longstanding hypertension has plasma sodium 130 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 268, urine osmolality 720 mOsm/kg, and is clinically euvolemic. He has had this lab pattern for years and is asymptomatic. His ADH increases appropriately with further water loading and decreases with water deprivation, but the threshold appears shifted. Which of the following best characterizes 'reset osmostat'?
choices: Reset osmostat — stable shifted set point for ADH regulation
Reset osmostat is a synonym for SIADH
Reset osmostat features inappropriate ADH suppression
Reset osmostat is acute and progressive
explanations: Correct. Reset osmostat is a chronic condition in which the osmotic set point for ADH secretion is SHIFTED to a lower-than-normal level — the patient regulates plasma sodium at, say, 130 (instead of 140) but with all the normal regulatory machinery intact. ADH responds appropriately above the new threshold (rises with rising Posm, falls with falling Posm). Patients can DILUTE urine when water-loaded (demonstrating preserved suppression), unlike SIADH where this is impaired. Plasma sodium is stable in the low-normal to mildly-low range without progression and without symptoms (because the set point was reached). Common in chronic illness, malignancy, chronic malnutrition, pregnancy, quadriplegia. Often INCIDENTAL finding; usually does NOT require treatment unless symptomatic.
Incorrect. SIADH features INAPPROPRIATE ADH despite low Posm; reset osmostat features appropriate ADH for the new set point.
Incorrect. Reset osmostat features APPROPRIATE ADH regulation around a new set point — not inappropriate suppression.
Incorrect. Reset osmostat causes mild HYPONATREMIA (~130), not hypernatremia.
Incorrect. Reset osmostat is CHRONIC and STABLE, not acute and progressive.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in her 24th week of pregnancy has plasma sodium 134 mEq/L (lower than her pre-pregnancy baseline of 140). She is otherwise healthy and asymptomatic. Which of the following best explains the changes in water regulation during pregnancy?
choices: Pregnancy has no effect on water regulation
Pregnancy lowers the osmotic threshold for ADH secretion
explanations: Incorrect. Pregnancy is NOT associated with SIADH; the lower threshold is physiologic, not pathologic.
Incorrect. Pregnancy can transiently cause central DI in late pregnancy (placental vasopressinase) but not nephrogenic DI as a typical feature.
Incorrect. Pregnancy LOWERS, not raises, the ADH threshold.
Incorrect. Pregnancy has well-recognized effects on water regulation.

Correct. Pregnancy is associated with several adaptive changes in water regulation: (1) The osmotic threshold for ADH secretion is LOWERED by ~10 mOsm/kg, mediated by hCG and progesterone effects on hypothalamic osmoreceptors. (2) The thirst threshold is correspondingly lowered. The result is a 'physiologic reset osmostat' — pregnant women regulate their plasma sodium at ~135 (instead of 140) but with all regulatory machinery intact. This stable mild hyponatremia is BENIGN, requires no treatment, and resolves postpartum. (3) In LATE pregnancy, placental vasopressinase (cysteine aminopeptidase) accelerates ADH metabolism, occasionally unmasking transient central DI in women with marginal posterior pituitary function. Treatment: desmopressin (resistant to vasopressinase) is effective; vasopressin would not work. Resolves postpartum within 4–6 weeks. Recognition is important to avoid misdiagnosis as SIADH or other states.
